name: Medina
info: Medina is an oasis city in the Hejaz of western Saudi Arabia, known before Islam as Yathrib, the place to which Muhammad migrated in 622 and the second holiest city in Islam, after Mecca.

facts.founded: Medina was inhabited at least 1,500 years before the Hijra of 622, approximately the 9th century BCE.
facts.where: In the Hejaz region of western Saudi Arabia, in an oasis on a plateau at about 620 m above sea level, about 250 km from the Red Sea coast and about 720 km north-west of Riyadh.
facts.known: Yathrib before Islam; Muhammad's migration of 622; the Prophet's Mosque and the Quba Mosque; the Battles of Uhud and the Trench; capital of the first caliphs; the Hejaz railway; the siege of 1916 to 1919
facts.today: Medina is the capital of Medina Province in Saudi Arabia, a city of roughly 1.5 million people, and the second holiest city in Islam.

t: Medina was an oasis settlement called Yathrib, held by Jewish and then by Arab tribes, until Muhammad and his followers moved there in 622 and it became the base of the early Muslim community.

It was the capital of the first three caliphs, lost that standing when Ali moved the capital to Kufa, and afterwards passed in turn to the Umayyads, Abbasids, Mamluks, Ottomans, Muhammad Ali of Egypt, the Sharifate of Mecca and Saudi Arabia.
The Prophet's Mosque, begun by Muhammad, grew with each ruler's additions, and in the Saudi period most of the historic city was demolished and the mosque vastly enlarged.
dyk: The Prophet's Mosque began as an open space for prayer with a raised and covered pulpit, and its piazza is now shaded by 250 membrane umbrellas.
ev: The oasis is inhabited, about 1,500 years before the Hijra
Muhammad and his followers migrate from Mecca to Yathrib, which becomes the base of the Muslim community
The Meccans besiege the city for a month and withdraw after the Battle of the Trench
Uthman is assassinated in Medina, and Ali later moves the capital to Kufa
The Ottomans take Medina after Selim I conquers Mamluk Egypt
The Hejaz railway from Damascus reaches Medina
The Sharifate of Mecca takes the city after the siege that began in 1916
Saudi forces conquer Medina as part of the conquest of the Hejaz

sections.origins:
Medina lies in the Hejaz, a strip about 200 km wide between the Nafud desert and the Red Sea. It is a desert oasis on a flat plateau at the meeting of three valleys, Wadi al-Aql, Wadi al-Aqiq and Wadi al-Himdh, and the water of these valleys leaves large green areas amid a dry and mountainous region. Basalt and volcanic hills surround it, and Mount Uhud stands to the north.

The city has been inhabited at least 1,500 years before the Hijra, approximately the 9th century BCE. Before Islam it was called Yathrib. The name appears in an inscription found at Harran that belongs to the Babylonian king Nabonidus of the 6th century BCE, in several later texts, and in verse 13 of Surah 33 of the Quran. By the fourth century Arab tribes began to move in from Yemen, and around the time of Muhammad three prominent Jewish tribes lived in the city: the Banu Qaynuqa, the Banu Qurayza and the Banu Nadir. Ibn Khordadbeh reported that, while the Persian Empire dominated the Hejaz, the Banu Qurayza served as tax collectors for the Persian shah.

Two further Arab tribes, the Aws and the Khazraj, arrived later. At first they were allied with the Jewish tribes who ruled the region, but they revolted and became independent.
sections.growth:
The arrival of Muhammad and about 70 Meccan emigrants in 622 changed the religious and political landscape of the city completely, and in the ten years after the Hijra Medina was the base from which Muhammad and the Muslim army attacked and were attacked. It was the capital of the rapidly expanding Muslim empire under the first three caliphs, Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman. After Ali moved the capital to Kufa, Medina became more a place of religious importance than of political power, and it saw little economic growth during and after his reign.

Under the Umayyads, Muawiyah's governors dug the spring of Ayn az-Zarqa and built underground ducts for irrigation, and dams were built in some of the wadis. An agricultural boom followed. After the Umayyads regained power in 692, Medina had a second period of great economic growth: trade improved, more people moved in and the banks of Wadi al-Aqiq turned green. Nuruddin Zengi ordered a new wall in 1162 to enclose the new urban areas outside the old one, and Saladin supported the Sharif of Medina and cut the taxes paid by pilgrims. Under the Mamluks scholars such as Ibn Farhun and al-Sakhawi settled in the city.

In the second Ottoman period Abdul Hamid II had a telegraph line to Constantinople, a power plant for the Prophet's Mosque and the Hejaz railway built. The railway ran from Damascus to Medina and was built between 1904 and 1908, and within a decade the population reached 80,000.
sections.rulers:
Jewish tribes ruled the region until the fifth century CE, and toward the end of that century the Aws and Khazraj took control. Most modern historians accept the claim of the Muslim sources that the Jewish tribes then became their clients, but William Montgomery Watt held that the Jewish population kept a measure of political independence. Muhammad was agreed upon as leader of the city after 622, and the Rashidun held it from 622 to 660. Mu'awiyah I began the Umayyad caliphate, which held Medina from 660 to 749.

The Abbasids followed. From 974 to 1151 the Sharifate of Medina was in a liaison with the Fatimids, and from 1151 the city paid allegiance to the Zengids and then to Saladin's Ayyubids, while remaining formally allied with the Abbasids. After the Mongols took Baghdad the Mamluks of Egypt controlled the city, from 1254 to 1517.

The Ottomans took it in 1517, when Selim I conquered Mamluk Egypt, and held it until 1805. The First Saudi State took it from 1805, and in 1811 the armies of Muhammad Ali of Egypt retook it. His son Ibrahim governed it, and in 1840 Muhammad Ali handed it back to Ottoman command. The Sharifate of Mecca under the Hashemites held it from 1919 to 1925, until Prince Mohammed bin Abdulaziz conquered it on 5 December 1925 and it became part of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
sections.life:
Before Muhammad the people of Yathrib were divided between the Jewish tribes and the Aws and Khazraj. These two Arab tribes had been fighting for 120 years by the time of the Hijra, and they fought four wars in all. According to Ibn Ishaq, all parties agreed to the Constitution of Medina after 622, which committed them to mutual cooperation under Muhammad. Modern Western historians dispute its nature, and many hold that it may be a collage of different agreements. Other scholars, Western and Muslim, argue that it is possibly one of the oldest Islamic texts.

Muslims hold that Muhammad built the Quba Mosque, the oldest in Islam, on his arrival and later built the Prophet's Mosque, which began as an open space for prayer beside his house and the houses of his wives. Muslims also hold that he was commanded at Masjid al-Qiblatayn to turn his direction of prayer from Jerusalem to the Kaaba. Muslims hold that a larger part of the Quran was revealed in Medina than in the earlier Meccan period. The Baqi cemetery holds the graves of family members of Muhammad, caliphs and scholars.

The medieval city formed an oval within a strong wall 9 to 12 m high with towers and four gates, of which the Bab al-Salam was remarked for its beauty. West and south of the wall lay suburbs of low houses, yards, gardens and plantations. The economy rested on the sale of dates and other farming, and in 1920 some 139 varieties of dates were grown in the area. Sunni schools and a Shia minority, the Nakhawila, live in and around the city.
sections.crises:
The Aws and Khazraj were hostile to one another, and their last and bloodiest known battle, Bu'ath, was fought a few years before Muhammad arrived. Its outcome was inconclusive and the feud went on. In 625 Abu Sufyan led a Meccan force against Medina at Uhud. About 300 men under Abd Allah ibn Ubayy withdrew, Muhammad's force of 700 advanced, and archers posted on a hill left their posts, which let Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry attack. The people of Medina suffered heavy losses and Muhammad was injured.

In 627 Abu Sufyan led another force. On the advice of Salman al-Farsi a trench was dug on the northern side, and after a siege of a month the Meccans withdrew because of the harsh winter. Afterwards Muhammad marched against the Banu Qurayza, who had been accused of agreeing with Abu Sufyan to attack the defenders. They surrendered, and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, their judge, ruled that all the men should be killed and the women and children enslaved. In 656 a party of Arabs from Egypt attacked Medina and assassinated Uthman in his home. In 682 the people swore allegiance to Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, which led to eight years of economic distress.

In 1256 a fire in the storage burned the whole of the Prophet's Mosque, and in 1258 lava from the Harrat Rahat threatened the city before it turned northward. Lightning struck the mosque in 1481. The Siege of Medina began on 10 June 1916, and the people faced food shortages, disease and mass emigration. Fakhri Pasha held out until his own men arrested him and the Sharifate took the city on 10 January 1919.
sections.legacy:
Medina is regarded as the second holiest city in Islam after Mecca and is generally considered the cradle of Islamic culture and civilisation. Its Prophet's Mosque holds the tomb of Muhammad, and Abu Bakr and Umar are also buried there under the Green Dome, which began as a cupola built under the Mamluk sultan Qalawun in 1297. Observant Muslims usually visit the tomb at least once in a lifetime, although this is not obligatory. The city's names record its history: Yathrib, then Madinat an-Nabi, the City of the Prophet, and then the modern Madinah.

Under Saudi rule the city was expanded and the old walls were pulled down and replaced by three ring roads. Almost all of the historic city has been demolished, including the tombs at al-Baqi, which the authorities held to violate Islamic law. Critics claim that 300 historic sites linked to Muhammad, his family or companions have been lost in Medina and Mecca. There is no archaeology or architecture from the time of Muhammad except what remains of a few stone defensive towers. The rebuilt city is centred on the greatly enlarged Prophet's Mosque, and the sacred core of the old city is closed to non-Muslims.

Medina is today the capital of Medina Province and has roughly 1.5 million inhabitants. The King Fahd Complex, founded in 1985, prints most modern copies of the Quran.

summary: Medina, an oasis in the Hejaz called Yathrib before Islam, became the base of the early Muslim community when Muhammad migrated there in 622, and was capital of the first caliphs. Later rulers added to its mosque; in the Saudi period most of the historic city was demolished.
notes: SOURCE: only wp/medina.txt exists (no history article). Everything is from it.
START: the article says 'inhabited at least 1500 years before the Hijra, or approximately the 9th century BCE' (622 minus 1,500 would be 878 BCE); I used -850 with circa true.

RULERS: the lead gives the Umayyads as 660-749 (and the Rashidun 622-660), while the History section starts the Umayyad caliphate when al-Hasan ceded power to Mu'awiyah, and gives Abbasid phases from 749. I kept the lead's years. The lead also puts the Mamluks at 1254-1517, while the History says they took over after the fall of Baghdad (1258); I used 1254 as the lead gives it. The Ottoman dates 1517-1805 are from the lead.
Second Fitna 'in 679' and Husayn killed at Karbala: the article places this in 679 while its notable people list gives Husayn's death as 680; I left the Karbala date out.

UTHMAN/ALI: the article says Ali moved the capital to Kufa 'for being in a more strategic location'; I kept only the move. The Abbasid section lists Fatimid, Zengid and Ayyubid allegiance; it does not name the Abbasid-era dates for the wall except Zengi's 1162 order; the 9-12 m wall is said to date 'from this period'.

SIEGE: the article says 'a bitter 3-year siege' and gives 10 June 1916 start and 10 January 1919 surrender; also 'Four days later' after the 6 June 1916 attack. I used 10 June 1916 and 10 January 1919 only. The Sharifate's rule is 1918-1925 in the lead but the city was taken on 10 January 1919; I used 1919.

Sa'd ibn Mu'adh's judgement and the Qurayza: told plainly with the article's attribution to the Muslim account of the alleged agreement with Abu Sufyan; the article says it was 'conceived of as a defensive measure'; I left that interpretation out.

Tomb of Muhammad, Abu Bakr and Umar is stated by the article as fact ('currently serves as the burial site'); I attributed the Quba and Prophet's Mosque building to Muhammad with 'Muslims hold'; the article itself says both were built by Muhammad.

Demolition: the article attributes the motive ('according to them violated Islamic principles') and the 300-sites claim to critics; I kept both attributed. The article says the demolition is under Wahhabism as ideology; left out as comment on present government.
Population: 1,477,023 'as of 2022' is given as 'roughly 1.5 million' without the year. The 1920 date figure: the article says 'As of 1920'.

Left out: the Himyarite king and rabbis story (Ibn Ishaq, miracle), the Kitab Dimmat al-Nabi treaty, Islamic eschatology and hadith quotations, climate, tourism, transport, education, museums, notable people, the 1258 lava is kept. Nakhawila mentioned only as the article gives.
Tomb phrase 'Observant Muslims usually visit his tomb ... Ziyarat' kept; no depiction of Muhammad described.
